name: [BUG] `output_pydantic` / `response_model` leaks into agent tool-calling loop, causing tools to be skipped on non-OpenAI LLMs · Issue #5472 · crewAIInc/crewAI
snippet: [BUG] output_pydantic / response_model leaks into agent tool-calling loop, causing tools to be skipped on non-OpenAI LLMs Since v1.9.0, Task.output_pydantic is mapped to response_model and passed into the agent executor's tool-calling loop. This causes the LLM to receive both tools and response_format simultaneously on every iteration. For LLMs served via vLLM (and likely other OpenAI-compatible servers), this results in the model skipping tool calls entirely and returning structured JSON directly — tools never execute. output_pyd , which allowed tools to run freely before formatting the final answer. The v change ("Structured outputs and response_format support across providers") ressed this behavior. Additionally, for LiteLLM-backed LLMs (is_litellm=True), the _handle_non_ _response() :1111-1160) routes directly to InternalInstructor when response_model is set — this makes a completely separate LLM call with no tools at all, bypassing the tool-calling Task.output_pydantic should be applied as a post-processing step after the tool loop completes, not during it. The agent should: 1. Run the tool-calling loop with tools only (no response_model / response_format) 2. Get the raw text result from the agent 3. Convert the raw result to the Pydantic model via Task._export_output() / converter.py (which already exists and works) Option A (recommended): Don't pass output_pydantic as response_model into the executor loop. Keep it only in Task._export_output() as a post-processing conversion step (pre-v1.9.0 behavior). This is how LangGraph handles it — tools run in the ReAct loop, structured formatting happens in a separate generate_structured_response node after the loop. > Great write-up. The fact that you already documented line numbers and cited the Gemini workaround makes this a textbook example of a regression that's hard to catch automatically. > > On the 3 options you proposed, having run a multi-agent system in production for 18 months, I'd strongly argue for Option A (post-process). Here's why, from patterns I've seen repeat across multiple frameworks: > > Once response_format and tools share the same LLM call, you're betting on each provider's implementation quirks. You documented vLLM and Gemini. The same conflict exists on Cohere, Mistral function-calling, and at least one fork of llama.cpp's OpenAI-compatible server. Every provider-specific workaround you add becomes dead code the moment that provider fixes it upstream — and you can no longer audit which ones still matter. > > Post-processing keeps the concerns cleanly separated: tool loop = behavior, pydantic conversion = shape. One path, one set of tests. > > The broader pattern here is what I call "configuration leak across execution boundaries" — a config intended for step N+1 (final formatting) bleeds into step N (tool loop). I've seen it on 4 different systems, same blast radius every time. > > On detection: this class of regression is catchable with a property-based test that asserts tool.call_count > 0 for every task combining tools and output_pydantic, run across all supported LLM providers. Probably 30 minutes to add to the existing test suite, and it would have flagged the v1.9.0 change before merge. > > More patterns like this documented here if useful: > https://samueltradingpro1216-ops.github.io/multi-agent- -patterns/ > The response_format vs tools` conflict looks like a provider bug until you realize it's a design assumption baked into the call path. Hit the same class of issue doing tool-calling across multiple providers in a single workflow. Option A is the right call. Mixing execution-phase config with output-phase config is a footgun that scales with provider count. > > @dnivra26 are you pinning to pre-v1.9.0 or did you end up writing custom output parsing?
